Distinguished delegates, the report notes that in the 20 years that have passed since the World Summit on the Information Society established a people-centered, inclusive, and development-oriented framework for harnessing the potential of digital technologies, progress has been significant, but digital divides remain within and among countries. The report notes the continued relevance of this vision as we approach the conclusion of the WISES+20 review in December. This review provides a crucial opportunity to take stock of achievements and gaps and to ensure effective collaboration with other processes, including the implementation of the GDC, so that our collaborative efforts are coherent, avoid unnecessary duplication, and align with the broader objectives of sustainable development. In this regard, and in preparation of the WSIS+20 review, the ECOSOC requested the CSTD to gather multi-stakeholder inputs, conduct substantive discussions, and consider the findings at its 28th session in April 25. I am pleased to report that the CSTD has submitted to the General Assembly, through the ECOSOC, the results of its WSIS+20 work, as well as a report by the UNTAD Secretariat, which will inform, we hope, the discussion of the WSIS+20 review. Before concluding, I would like to note that the Secretary-General's report highlights the promise of rapid advances in artificial intelligence alongside other frontier technologies, including boosting productivity and enhancing essential services such as education, health, and commerce. At the same time, the pace of technological progress has exceeded initial expectations, bringing with it a range of complex challenges. In addition to increasing investment in public digital infrastructure, the expansion of the government services and the development of digital skills, member states may also wish to prioritize policies that address risks associated with digitalization, which includes cybersecurity, disinformation, surveillance and environmental impacts, while ensuring the governance of frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence and robotics is ethical, inclusive and development-oriented. Let me move now to the report of the Secretary General on Science, Technology and Innovation for Sustainable Development. This report provides information on the implementation of GA resolution 78/160. The report discusses the role of science, technology and innovation in addressing multiple crises and reducing poverty. It underlines that science, technology and innovation offers transformative solutions to foster the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and to address multiple crises facing the world. The first key message of the report is that seizing those opportunities requires domestic action backed by international collaboration and support. The second message is that countries need to harness effectively both mature technologies and newer frontier technologies which are evolving quickly and are resulting in profound global changes. Technologies such as artificial intelligence offer huge benefits for transformation and diversification, productivity, growth, and competitiveness, but also create new risks. Third, the report argues that new technology divides are opening up across and within countries with the rapid development of frontier technologies. Developing countries require improved innovation systems, stronger scientific, technological, and innovation capabilities. better infrastructure, increased funding, and effective technology transfer and absorption. Fourth, technological advancements are reshaping economic diversification opportunities, challenging export-oriented models, and fueling a shift towards knowledge-intensive and digital-driven growth. As the global economy moves towards services and digitalization, it is essential to rethink industrial and innovation policies to drive the structural transformation and industrial upgrading. Lastly, digital frontier technologies offer developing countries new opportunities to diversify their economies through three key channels. First, enhancing productivity and boosting export growth. Second, fostering new industries such as telemedicine or electronic commerce. And third, promoting a green and digital transition through efficiency and the emergence of new green industries. However, as noted before, digitalization also presents risks, including the potential for re-shoring that could undermine developing countries' participation in global value chains, a reduction in demand for lower-skilled labor, and a widening productivity gap due to barriers to accessing new digital technologies. Looking ahead, the report underscores the role of technology assessment and technology foresight exercises in helping countries understand and set the implications of technologies for socioeconomic systems and sustainable development. Together, these practices support a comprehensive framework for national decision making, enabling a strategic forward-looking evidence-based policy and building capacity for anticipatory technology governance. The report suggests that an international mechanism to facilitate technology foresight and technology assessment is highly desirable. The report also argues that international cooperation on frontier technologies, especially AI, is essential and recommends the governments establish international guidance on AI development that favors the public interest by developing consistent normative frameworks, ethical guidelines, standards, and regulations on frontier technologies. All countries have a stake in the future of AI, but very few have influence over the direction that it's taking, which may result in a failure of global AI governance. The report calls for multi-stakeholder cooperation to make AI accessible and beneficial for everyone, and to foster inclusive innovation in tackling global challenges. In conclusion, the report highlights six specific areas for stronger STI collaboration at the international level. First, reinforcing efforts to build an inclusive global STI agenda. Second, developing a multilateral STI foresight and assessment system. Third, building enabling digital skills environments. Fourth, fostering investment in STI and public-private partnerships. Fifth, strengthening research networks and collaboration among different actors. And finally, promoting technology and knowledge transfer. Thank you very much for your attention.

Thank you, Madam Chair, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. As requested by the General Assembly resolution 78/162, this report A/80/418 presents an in-depth analysis of the support available to middle-income countries in their pursuit of inclusive and just transition pathways for sustainable development, including the impact of new and inclusive development approaches. Such support is more important than ever. Although MICs, or middle-income countries, as a group have made great progress towards sustainable development, multiple challenges are reshaping previously established development pathways. Large-scale climate disruptions, changing trade relationships, and rapid technological change, including the onset of AI, all exacerbate structural barriers to sustainable development. At the same time, mixed response capacities are being strained. Average economic growth across this group is expected to turn out at about 4.2% over 2024 to 2026, well below the pre-pandemic average of 5.6%. Fiscal space has shrunk, public debt burdens are going up, and there's mounting debt service payments which crowd out investments in sustainable development. As of July 2025, the middle-income country category comprises 104 economies with gross national income per capita ranging from $1,136 to $13,935. This spectrum reflects the diversity of economic structures, capacities and development challenges within the group. For instance, economic growth in mix has not always corresponded with a marked increase decrease in multidimensional poverty. Persistent gender inequality remains a challenge in many. and the multidimensional vulnerability index shows that there are 24 MICS among the one-third most vulnerable countries worldwide. Distinguished delegate, the report also draws on the high-level meeting convened by the President of the General Assembly on the 1st of April, 2025, under the theme addressing structural barriers to sustainable development in middle-income countries. Key messages from the meeting include the urgency of adopting new development frameworks that move beyond GDP and the importance of strengthening tailored international support, including access to finance, technology, capacity building, and the critical role of South-South and triangular cooperation. The analytical findings of this report reinforce these messages. New development pathways would be characterized by economics transformation, expansion to low carbon sectors, changed food systems, inclusive labor markets, technical innovation, digitalization, well-developed human capital, and social dialogue to ensure that no one is left behind. Such transformations require integrated policies that advance economic prosperity while embedding social inclusion and environmental stewardship. Policymakers must harness technological advancements and strengthen institutional capacities, paying special attention to the inclusion of women and girls and people, groups and vulnerable situations. However, makes face significant financing gaps for capital investments, even as they are addressing their current spending needs. The report therefore calls for. Greater multilateral support, including concessional financing based on multidimensional vulnerabilities and adherence to new collective quantified goal on climate finance agreed at COP 29, which commits developed countries to deliver at least 300 billion annually to developing countries by 2035. Additional efforts towards reforming the international debt architecture with concrete actions, including strengthening of debt management, debt transparency, responsible borrowing and lending, significant lowering of borrowing costs, restoration of debt sustainability, including through a review of the sovereign debt architecture, and the harnessing of technological advancements, strengthening of institutional capacities, enhancing social protection in support of just and sustainable transitions. The support of the United Nations development system is reflected in country level expenditures of which mix account for over 50% as highlighted by the report. UN support is also becoming more targeted with improved strategies, refined indicators, and stronger alignment with national priorities. This alignment should be further strengthened through inclusive, nationally led coordination platforms that bring together key stakeholders with the UN in a central and coordinating role, as envisaged already in the Ceville commitment. Ladies and gentlemen, these are challenging times for development cooperation. And while numbers are not yet available by income group, recent trends show a steady decline in mixed share of total ODA. Resolution 78/162 has called for advancing the elaboration of a specific interagency comprehensive system-wide response plan for mix, which needs to be informed by consistent in-depth analysis of their evolving vulnerabilities, development trajectories, and opportunities. DESA has initiated preparations to advance this elaboration. The current juncture also presents a need and an opportunity to strengthen South-South and triangular cooperation, while recognizing that it cannot substitute for traditional North-South cooperation. Unlocking this potential requires a comprehensive approach that is also nuanced enough to address individual entrenched challenges, a strategic plan of action, as also called for in the 2024 Rabat Declaration and reiterated in the 2025 Makati Declaration adopted by high-level ministerial conferences on middle-income countries. This concludes my brief overview of this report. As always, we stand ready to support your deliberations on this topic. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the United Republic of Tanzania, and I now give the floor to His Excellency, Permanent Representative of Timor-Leste.

Madam Chair, thank you for giving me the floor. Information and communication technology has been transformative force in fostering globalization and driving sustainable development. It serves as a cornerstone for connecting economies, cultures, and populations in unprecedented ways. However, while ICT presents immense opportunities, its benefits are not shared equally. Many vulnerable nations, including small island developing states and least developed countries, continue to face persistent challenges related to infrastructure, affordability, and digital literacy. In June 2023, the government of Timor-Leste launched Timor Digital 2032, a national strategy plan designed to harness digital technologies to strengthen governance, diversify the economy, and advance priority sectors, including health, education, and agriculture. This plan is currently being updated to formally integrate artificial intelligence, reflecting our commitment to keeping pace with technological advancements. A central pillar of this transformation is the South Submarine Cable Project, a 607-kilometer government-funded initiative connecting Dili to Australia's Northwest Cable System, with a capacity of 27 terabytes per second. The cable landed in June 2024 and became ready for service in 2025. marking Timor-Leste's first international submarine linkage. This milestone has already expanded access to faster, more reliable, and affordable internet, linking Timor-Leste more closely with Southeast Asia and the global digital economy. These infrastructure gains are already generating momentum. UNTAD's readiness assessment Timor-Leste highlight Timor-Leste growing e-commerce potential with strategy implementation of Timor Digital 2032 and sustained investment. Timor-Leste aims to enhance this development to improve the quality of life for all citizens and accelerate sustainable development. Sure, Timor-Leste experience demonstrate both the vulnerability and the opportunistic phase.

Mr. Chair. Madam Chair, the rapidly evolving landscape of science and ICTs hold transformative potential to drive economic growth and entrepreneurship, enhance e-governance services, and reduce poverty and inequality. Yet, we remain deeply concerned about the widening global economic and digital divides, escalating cybercrimes, and the misuse of digital platforms for extremism, online violence, and misinformation. Chair, Nepal accords utmost priority to leveraging STIs and ICTs as an enabler for attaining SDGs, accelerating sustainable development, and improving quality of life of our peoples. Our development policy underscores the need to expand ICT access, promote investment in scientific research, and utilize these advancements for economic transformation and national development. In pursuit of this vision, Nepal has declared the decade from 2024 to 2034 as the IT decade. We stress developing robust digital public infrastructure, expanding broadband connectivity, and enhancing inclusive access to technologies. In this context, first, closing the digital divide between and among nations must remain a collective global priority. The fact that Over 2.6 billion people, nearly one third of the humanity, remains offline, underlines this urgency. Mobilizing FDI, development assistance, and domestic resources alongside sound data governance, intellectual property protection, and competition frameworks can help address existing gaps. Nepal stands ready to partner with the international community to harness ICTs and SDI for a just, inclusive, and sustainable digital future for all. Thank you.

Thank you, Chair, Excellencies. Science, technology, and innovation are powerful enablers of sustainable development. Around the world, there is growing interest in mission-oriented innovation, an approach that requires public leadership to shape markets and steer portfolios of solutions across sectors and technologies. Through our cross-directorate initiative, the OECD Mission Action Lab, we are supporting countries in designing and implementing mission-oriented STI strategies. This includes work with OECD members and the European Union, as well as partnerships with middle income countries, aligning SDI investments with digital inclusion goals. Our experience shows that sustained investment and strategic direction are essential, and that SDI systems must be retooled to be truly fit for purpose in driving transformative change. A key area of focus is digital public infrastructure, secure, interoperable systems that enable broad access to public and private services. DPI includes digital identity, data sharing systems, digital payments, and digital notifications. These systems are foundational for inclusive economic and social development. To support this, we are identifying good practices across OECD countries and establishing a platform for peer learning and collaboration among developing cooperation providers, UN agencies, and government partners from low and middle income countries. During turning to developing cooperation with middle income countries, the OECD Development Assistance Committee is enhancing cooperation with middle income countries to support sustainable transitions beyond official development assistance eligibility. Under the strengthened graduation framework, potential graduates are encouraged to develop country led strategies with donor partners to ensure a smooth phase out of official development assistance, foster new forms of cooperation and safeguard development gains as part of this effort, the OECD will contact country pilots. Costa Rica and Panama, supported by the OECD, are two countries that are currently implementing such strengthened graduation strategies, ensuring financing sustainability. These efforts build on the Seville Commitment and Platform for Action, focusing on resilience, domestic resource mobilization, and innovative partnership. Thank you very much, Chair.
